{{nihongo|'''Toshi Shrine'''|利神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in {{ill|Kakegawa, Shizuoka|Q823988|qid=Q823988}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|Q131320|qid=Q131320}}. Under the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=ancient shrine ranking system}}, its {{ill|Shakaku|Q10444029|qid=Q10444029}} is {{ill|Shikinai Shosha|Q134917287|qid=Q134917287}}. Under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, its rank is {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|qid=Q134917316}}. {{nihongo|'''Toshi Shrine'''|利神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Tōtōmi Province]].

== Overview ==
It is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in Shimomata-Minami, {{ill|Kakegawa, Shizuoka|Q823988|qid=Q823988}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|Q131320|qid=Q131320}}<ref name="nta20151113"/><ref>“Toshi Shrine,” “[http://www.shizuoka-jinjacho.or.jp/shokai/jinja.php?id=4409002 Toshi Shrine - Shizuoka Prefectural Association of Shinto Shrines]” {{ill|Shizuoka Prefectural Shrine Association|Q134956727|qid=Q134956727}}.</ref>. It enshrines two deities, {{ill|Toshigami|Q3028663|qid=Q3028663}} and {{ill|Ukanomitama|lt=Ukanomitama-no-Kami|Q3080728|qid=Q3080728}}<ref name="shikinaishaToshiJinja"/><ref name="mre1925_289"/>, and counts as its {{ill|Ujiko|Q125562175|qid=Q125562175}} the residents of the Shimomata-chō Ward, Chūō 2-chōme Ward, Jūkyūshu Ward, Odaka-chō Ward, Chūō 3-chōme Ward, and Chūō-Takamachi Ward, which are districts of Kakegawa City<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. It is identified with the “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;” listed as a {{ill|Shikinai Shosha|Q134917287|qid=Q134917287}} in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932}}<ref name="masamune1929_128">{{ill|Masamune Atsuo|Q3297160|qid=Q3297160}} (ed.), “Engishiki,” vol. 2, Nihon Koten Zenshū Kankōkai, 1929, p. 128.</ref><ref name="mre1925_289"/><ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. During the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963}}, it held joint festivals together with {{ill|Tatsuo Shrine|Q11679232|qid=Q11679232}} and {{ill|Shinmei-gū|Q118146837|qid=Q118146837|lt=Shinmei Shrine}}<ref name="kakegawa201801_77">{{ill|Kakegawa City Office|Q109594222|qid=Q109594222|lt=Kakegawa City}} “Kakegawa City Plan for the Maintenance and Improvement of Historic Landscape,” January 2018, p. 77.</ref>, which is known as the origin of today’s {{ill|Kakegawa Matsuri|Q11498235|qid=Q11498235}}<ref name="kakegawa201801_77"/>.

== Enshrined deities ==
* {{ill|Toshigami|Q3028663|qid=Q3028663}}<ref name="shikinaishaToshiJinja"/><ref name="mre1925_289"/>
* {{ill|Ukanomitama|lt=Ukanomitama-no-Kami|Q3080728|qid=Q3080728}}<ref name="shikinaishaToshiJinja"/><ref name="mre1925_289"/>

== History ==
The date of its founding is unknown<ref name="shikinaishaToshiJinja"/><ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. However, since “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;” is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai Shosha|Q134917287|qid=Q134917287|lt=minor shrine}} of {{ill|Saya district|Q11385111|qid=Q11385111}} in volume 9 of the “{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}},” which was compiled in 927 ({{ill|Enchō|Q1327274|qid=Q1327274}} 5)<ref name="masamune1929_128"/><ref group="†">{{ill|Saya district|Q11385111|qid=Q11385111}} was merged with {{ill|Kitō district|Q11426221|qid=Q11426221}} to form {{ill|Ogasa District, Shizuoka|Q7079825|qid=Q7079825}} in 1896.</ref>, it is presumed that the shrine was founded prior to 927. The “Engishiki” is a legal code of the {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, compiled by {{ill|Fujiwara no Tokihira|Q2994735|qid=Q2994735}} and {{ill|Fujiwara no Tadahira|Q1397601|qid=Q1397601}} under the order of {{ill|Emperor Daigo|Q329753|qid=Q329753}}. The lists of shrines recorded in volumes 9 and 10 are known as the Engishiki Jinmyōchō, and the shrines listed therein were called {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}}.

In the Edo period, it was generously protected by the {{ill|Kakegawa Domain|Q3034456|qid=Q3034456}}<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/> and revered by the people as a guardian shrine of the western part of {{ill|Kakegawa-juku|Q3070229|qid=Q3070229}} in Sano District<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/><ref group="†">{{ill|Kakegawa-juku|Q3070229|qid=Q3070229}} and parts of Shimomata-chō, Jūkyūshu-chō, Nitō Village, Ōike Village, and Kuzukawa Village were merged in 1889 to establish {{ill|Kakegawa, Shizuoka|Q823988|qid=Q823988|lt=Kakegawa}}.</ref>. In 1743 (lunar calendar, {{ill|Kanpō|Q1145798|qid=Q1145798}} 3, 2nd month, 21st day), {{ill|Ogasawara Nagayuki|Q8515344|qid=Q8515344}}, heir to the domain lord, paid a visit<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>, and a record remains stating that he donated a pair of heishi (sake bottles) and one bu of gold on that occasion<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. A ridge tag also remains indicating that the main shrine was rebuilt in 1644 (lunar calendar, {{ill|Kanbun (era)|Q1146228|qid=Q1146228}} 4, 9th month)<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>.

Although records do not clearly indicate when the {{ill|Haiden (Shinto)|Q3125745|qid=Q3125745}} was roofed with tiles<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>, the buildings were rebuilt in 1915 ({{ill|Taishō era|Q329174|qid=Q329174}} 4)<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. In September 1926 (Taishō 15), the {{ill|Kagura-den|Q94498|qid=Q94498}} was rebuilt<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>.

== Examination regarding its status as a Shikinaisha ==
== Engishiki ==
[[File:Engishiki cropped Engishiki Vol 2 Flame 69.jpg|thumb|200px|The section in volume 9 of the “{{ill|Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448}}” included in the Nihon Koten Zenshū that mentions “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;”<ref name="masamune1929_128"/>]]
The shrine’s origin record clearly states that it is a “Shikinaisha”<ref name="shikinaishaToshiJinja"/>, and Toshi Shrine is regarded as the Shikinaisha listed in the Engishiki Jinmyōchō<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. However, since the Engishiki dates back to the Heian period, many Shikinaisha lost identifiable descendants over time. As a result, scholars of National Learning conducted long-term research to identify their successors, and the successor of the “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;” has been debated repeatedly. Regarding its reading, volume 9 of the Engishiki in the Nihon Koten Zenshū gives furigana reading “Toshino” for “Toshi”<ref name="masamune1929_128"/>.

== Jinmyōchō kōshō ==
[[File:Ban Nobutomo Zenshu cropped Ban Nobutomo Zenshu Vol 1 Frame 121.jpg|thumb|200px|A section in “&#xfa19;meichō Kōshō” included in the Ban Nobutomo Zenshū that discusses “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;”<ref name="ichishima1907_226">{{ill|Kenkichi Ichishima|Q11480125|qid=Q11480125}} (ed.), “Ban Nobutomo Zenshū,” vol. 1, {{ill|Kokusho Kankōkai (1905–1922)|Q28686029|qid=Q28686029}}, 1907, p. 226.</ref>]]
The Edo-period scholar {{ill|Ban Nobutomo|Q4346747|qid=Q4346747}} researched ancient shrines and authored “{{ill|Jinmyōchō Kōshō Dodai|Q11588823|qid=Q11588823|lt=Jinmyōchō Kōshō}}.” In it, he also discusses the “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;” of the Engishiki Jinmyōchō, introducing the theory that “west of Kakegawa-juku there is a place called Jūkyūshu, where there is Toshi Daimyōjin; this must be it”<ref name="ichishima1907_226"/>. Regarding its reading, he gives furigana “Tokami” for “Toshi”<ref name="ichishima1907_226"/>.

== Jinja Kakuroku ==
[[File:Jinja Kakuroku cropped Jinja Kakuroku Part Jo Frame 439.jpg|thumb|200px|A section in the upper volume of “{{ill|Jinja Kakuroku|Q11590708|qid=Q11590708|lt=&#xfa19;&#xfa4c; Kakuroku}}” discussing “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;”<ref name="suzuka1902_857">{{ill|Suzuka Tsuratane|Q6536446|qid=Q6536446|lt=Nakatomi no Asomi Tsugutane}} (sel.), “Tōtōmi Province,” authored by Suzuka Yoshikujira; edited by {{ill|Inoue Yorikuni|Q6535302|qid=Q6535302}} and {{ill|Saeki Ariyoshi|Q11382847|qid=Q11382847}}, “&#xfa19;&#xfa4c; Kakuroku,” upper volume, {{ill|Koten Kokyusho|Q11580997|qid=Q11580997}}, 1902, p. 857.</ref>]]
On the other hand, the Edo-period Shinto priest {{ill|Suzuka Tsuratane|Q6536446|qid=Q6536446}} also researched ancient shrines and authored the “{{ill|Jinja Kakuroku|Q11590708|qid=Q11590708}}.” Therein, he states regarding the “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;” of the Engishiki Jinmyōchō that the details of the enshrined deity and location were already unknown<ref name="suzuka1902_857"/>. He then introduces the same theory that “west of Kakegawa-juku there is a place called Jūkyūshu, where there is Toshi Daimyōjin; this must be it”<ref name="suzuka1902_857"/>. Regarding its reading, he states that “Toshi should be read as ‘To’”<ref name="suzuka1902_857"/>.

== Tokusen Shimmeichō ==
In the {{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period}}, research into ancient shrines also progressed within the {{ill|Ministry of Religion (Japan)|ja|教部省|ru|Министерство религий Японии|uk|Міністерство релігій Японії|qid=Q4294653}}, one of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=central government ministries}}, and the results were published as the “{{ill|Tokusen Jinmyōchō|Q11571092|qid=Q11571092}}.” In it, the location of the “Toshi &#xfa19;&#xfa4c;” of the Engishiki Jinmyōchō is clearly identified as “Kamegaya aza, Shimomata Village ({{ill|Ogasa District, Shizuoka|Q7079825|qid=Q7079825}}{{ill|Kakegawa, Shizuoka|Q823988|qid=Q823988|lt=Kakegawa}}{{ill|ōaza|Q424857|qid=Q424857}} Shimomata)”<ref name="mre1925_289"/>, making a definitive identification. Regarding its reading, furigana “Toshikami-no” is given for “Toshi”<ref name="mre1925_289"/>.

== Shrine precincts ==
Within the precincts stand a haiden with a heiden attached, covering the {{ill|Honden|Q2044994|qid=Q2044994}} of {{ill|Wood shingle|Q199388|qid=Q199388}} {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}} style<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>, as well as a kagura hall<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. Behind the precincts is Toshigami Pond<ref name="kakegawa201801_79"/>. Adjacent to the precincts is Toshigami Park<ref>“Toshigami Park,” “[https://www.city.kakegawa.shizuoka.jp/gyosei/docs/11065.html Toshigami Park - Kakegawa City]” {{ill|Kakegawa City Office|Q109594222|qid=Q109594222}}, November 21, 2014.</ref>.

== Festivals and annual events ==
Known festivals include the Gion Festival and the Autumn Festival. Prior to the Meiji period, the Gion Festival was held on June 15<ref name="kakegawa201801_80"/>, and the Autumn Festival on September 14<ref name="kakegawa201801_80"/>. From 1920 (Taishō 9), the Gion and Autumn festivals have been held jointly in October<ref name="kakegawa201801_80"/>.

Toshi Shrine also conducts the Kakegawa Festival as a joint festival of seven shrines together with Ryūbi Shrine, Shinmei Shrine, Ikebe Shrine, Hakusan Shrine, Tsushima Shrine, and Kifune Shrine<ref name="kakegawa201801_77"/>. Originally, the Kakegawa Festival originated from festivals jointly conducted by Toshi Shrine with Ryūbi Shrine and Shinmei Shrine<ref name="kakegawa201801_77"/>, and is said to have been held since the mid-Edo period<ref name="kakegawa201801_77"/>. In the Edo period, it was rare nationwide for multiple shrines to jointly conduct a festival<ref name="kakegawa201801_84">{{ill|Kakegawa City Office|Q109594222|qid=Q109594222|lt=Kakegawa City}} “Kakegawa City Plan for the Maintenance and Improvement of Historic Landscape,” January 2018, p. 84.</ref>. At the time, Kakegawa-juku was located within the sōguruwa (overall enclosure) of Kakegawa Castle<ref name="kakegawa201801_84"/>. As a result, unlike other castle towns, the samurai quarter and the post town were integrated<ref name="kakegawa201801_84"/>, and the parish areas of the three shrines—Ryūbi Shrine, Shinmei Shrine, and Toshi Shrine—were intermingled, which formed the background for this arrangement<ref name="kakegawa201801_84"/>.
